deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a continuous page of German lecture notes or excerpts on ancient history, section 'III. Babylonische Monarchie', second (Chaldean) period. It follows directly from the previous page (Nabopolassar, Necho) and continues onto the next (Cyrus 538, Babylonian trade, Phoenicians).

Content of this page, in order:
- The Chaldean conquerors met the Egyptian ones at the Euphrates. Nabopolassar was already old, and his son Nebuchadnezzar commanded the army.
- In 606 there was a decisive battle at Circesium on the Euphrates (i.e. Carchemish). Nebuchadnezzar defeated the (Egyptian) king and took all his conquered lands.
- As king, Nebuchadnezzar had already opened a way to conquests during his father's war. He allied with Media and took Nineveh, then expanded mainly westward. He pressed Phoenicia and besieged Tyre, which resisted most stubbornly.
- During the siege the inhabitants withdrew to nearby islands and founded New Tyre. Old Tyre was finally destroyed and its treasures carried to Babylon.
- He had already made Zedekiah of Judah a tributary. When Zedekiah rebelled and sought Egyptian help, Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem in 590 and deported the inhabitants into inner Asia.
- He made Babylon a great and splendid city. He is said to have become insane in his last years and to have recovered before dying in 562.
- The splendour of the Babylonian empire ended with him. The last king was Nabonadius (Nabonidus), at the time of Cyrus (next page).

The marginal underlined words are rubric names: 'Nebukadnezar' (repeated) and 'Zedekias'. There are no formulas, numbers to compute, or derivations, so nothing mathematical can be reconstructed.

The hand and the content (standard Göttingen-style ancient-history lecture material, Heeren-like) suggest student lecture notes. It is quite possibly not in Gauss's own hand, or it is a copy bound into the bundle.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics.

Historical dating follows older chronology. Carchemish (here 'Circesium') is now dated 605 BC, not 606. Jerusalem's fall is now 587/586 BC, not 590. Nebuchadnezzar's death in 562 BC is consistent with the modern date.
The capture of Nineveh (612 BC) was the work of Nabopolassar with the Medes, not of Nebuchadnezzar as king. The notes attribute it loosely to him.
The story of Nebuchadnezzar's madness comes from the Book of Daniel and is not historically attested. The notes hedge it with 'soll'.
